newsitem.title: CROATIA: U.N. condemns forged documents in Croatia enclave.
newsitem.headline: U.N. condemns forged documents in Croatia enclave.

text.p: U.N. transitional authorities in Croatia's last Serb enclave, Eastern Slavonia, on Friday condemned forged letters circulating in the region that seek information about alleged war criminals.

In a statement, the U.N. transitional administration (UNTAES) denounced what it called attempts to undermine its effort to prepare the region's return to Croatian government rule in a few months' time.

"UNTAES strongly condemns these provocative attempts to sow anxiety and insecurity among the residents of the region. Such acts are obviously intended to undermine UNTAES' mandate and the process of peaceful reintegration."

Purportedly issued by the U.N. war crimes tribunal, the letters sought information about 178 people said to be the subject of criminal proceedings. But the Hague-based court denied it had anything to do with such a document.
"The prosecutor, Justice Louise Arbour, states emphatically that this document did not originate from her office or from anyone within the tribunal," the tribunal said in a statement.
"It is a complete fabrication, and absolutely no credence should be attributed to it."
The statement also said Arbour planned to trace the source of the document and take "appropriate steps" against the perpetrators of the fraud.
UNTAES said postcards were also mailed to some local Serb residents explicitly urging them to "leave the region as soon as possible".

It pointed out that this was particularly detrimental to efforts to achieve reconciliation between local Serbs and Croats who will return to their former homes in Eastern Slavonia as part of the reintegration process.
"It also runs contrary to the main goals set up by the Government of Croatia for the successful completion of peaceful reintegration," it added.

UNTAES officials could not be reached for further comment on who might have forged the letters and why and spokesmen for the Croatian government were also unavailable on Friday, a public holiday in Croatia.

Minority Serbs seized Eastern Slavonia in a 1991 revolt against Croatia's secession from Yugoslavia but agreed to come back under Zagreb's authority after Croatian troops reconquered two other rebel Serb enclaves with ease in 1995.

Most of Eastern Slavonia's estimated 120,000 Serbs have since obtained Croatian citizenship papers in preparation for reintegration. But many embittered Croatian refugees set to return say co-existence with Serbs will be impossible, raising concern about revenge attacks once UNTAES leaves.
